I can answer the jetpack part. The answer comes in two parts: center of thrust and center of lift. A plane has an extremely precise center of lift and a nonchanging center of thrust. A little bit off forward or backward on the center of lift and it'd be rolling out of control, flipping out of control, or just generally not airworthy. The center of thrust also needs to be perfectly centered on the object. If the thrust was pushing a bit left or a bit right then you'd have the exact same sort of issues as one side of the vessel ends up getting pushed harder than another again resulting in out of control spins.

So now enter a human. In our center of lift is undefined and would constantly change depending on how we move our bodies. The center of thrust, relative to our bodies, would also be constantly changing - a small nudge away from center and it'd created a chain effect that would again result in a rapidly out of control spin.

This is why when you see professionals in jetpacks it's generally shaped similar to a plane to create a stable center of thrust/lift. The ones that are the traditional imagery of a jetpack (a sort of backpack with rear lift) are custom built to the pilot's body and said pilot is also going to stay extremely still while operating the device to maintain a stable center of lift/thrust. One hard sneeze and he'd be spinning out of control.

There's some possibilities like having a jetpack that that has mini thrusters as well that automatically fire to compensate for the pilot and ensure stability but that is incredibly complex and error prone, when again an error means you're going to go faceplant from however many meters up in the air you were.
